title: Goodwill for all
hookLine: Martin Luther King Jr. described agape as understanding, redeeming goodwill for all (Stride Toward Freedom)

cards: Black residents of Montgomery, Alabama, have stopped riding the city buses. Day after day they walk to work, in the cold and the rain. Their homes are threatened.
Their leaders are arrested. One of those leaders, a minister named Martin Luther King Jr., faces a hard question: how should the people feel about the ones doing this to them?
Later, in a book about those days called Stride Toward Freedom, he gave his answer. He reached for an old Greek word for love, and gave it a definition.

teach.b: King lays out three Greek words. Eros, a longing, even a love of beauty. Philia, the warm love between friends, who love each other back.
And agape, the one he means.
King describes agape as understanding, redeeming goodwill for all people. It doesn't wait to be earned, and it doesn't ask anything back.
It isn't liking: nobody is being asked to feel affection for the person who bombed their house. Agape is a settled will for the other person's good.
King writes that agape loves the person who does an evil deed while hating the deed itself. That's what made his kind of nonviolence different from simply staying quiet. The boycott kept pushing.

The goal, he says, was not to defeat or humiliate opponents, but to win their friendship and understanding. King, a Baptist minister, rooted this in the Gospels, and he credited Gandhi with showing him the method.
In the King James Bible, Jesus says: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you."
King's agape is that command, worked out in the streets of a real city, with real people on the other side.

how: In the nonviolent tradition Martin Luther King Jr. described, participants commit to opposing unjust deeds while seeking the good of their opponents, aiming at reconciliation rather than humiliation.

o: the warm love between friends who love each other back
a romantic longing drawn toward beauty and a beloved
goodwill that seeks everyone's good, even an opponent's

games.q: three words for love — tap the pairs.
p: goodwill for all, asking nothing back

s: King said agape means liking your opponents
he was clear it isn't liking or affection; it's goodwill for their good.
for King, agape loves the person while hating the evil deed
King said the boycott's goal was to humiliate opponents
he said the goal was to win their friendship and understanding.

games.q: you're in Montgomery, and someone has threatened your home. by King's agape, what are you asked to do?
o: oppose the deed, and still will their good.
stay quiet and stop the boycott.
games.why: agape isn't liking and isn't silence: the boycott kept pushing, while aiming to win the opponent's understanding.

practice: Bring to mind someone you're at odds with, not the hardest person in your life, someone medium: a coworker, a relative, a neighbor whose politics drive you up the wall.

You don't have to like them; just try King's distinction, set the deed to one side and look at the person, and without forcing a feeling, hold one simple wish for their good, that they're well, that they're understood.
If prayer is part of your life, let the wish go there too.

wordCard.voice: Agape. Martin Luther King Jr.'s word for understanding, redeeming goodwill for all people, even those who do you harm. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the love King described as understanding, redeeming goodwill for all.

carryVoice: Your line: win their friendship and understanding. Agape aims at the person's good, never their humiliation. That's day eight hundred fifty-six.

sources.ref: Martin Luther King Jr., Stride Toward Freedom, chapter on the pilgrimage to nonviolence

sources.q: Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you
